ReflectRL: Learning from Golden Negative Trajectories via Reflective-to-Direct Reasoning

Flawed expert trajectories become material for reflection, then a policy transition transfers the benefit to direct reasoning.

Bi Jinhe

August 4, 2026 ·Preprint ·3-minute read ·Read the paper ·PDF ·Code
1Why this matters 2How it works 3What the study finds 4What this means

The short version

ReflectRL studies expert trajectories that fail on difficult questions. Such trajectories need not be treated as correct demonstrations to contain useful information: they can provide a partially productive route that is easier to inspect and repair than to recreate from scratch. The study calls this setting a Reflection Advantage.

The framework uses these golden negative trajectories to elicit reflective reasoning, then transitions the policy back toward direct reasoning. This separates the information useful during training from the behavior desired when the trained model answers independently.

9Evaluation benchmarks
4Language-model backbones
4On-policy training methods

A failed expert attempt can retain useful structure when the learning objective rewards repairing it.

Why this matters

Trajectory-guided training loses supervision precisely where expert models also struggle. Discarding every failed attempt can remove intermediate reasoning structure that might still help a learner identify and resolve the difficult part.

How it works

  1. Collect failed expert trajectories as material for reflection rather than as targets to imitate.
  2. Combine reflective and direct reasoning within on-policy training.
  3. Apply a reflective-to-direct policy transition so the acquired behavior transfers to answering without trajectory guidance.

What the study finds

Experiments span nine benchmarks, four language-model backbones, and four on-policy training methods. Behavioral and intervention analyses examine the reflection advantage; training dynamics, ablations, and policy-transition comparisons test how the guidance affects learning and later direct reasoning.

What this means

This changes the role of a negative example from a scalar signal of failure to an object with potentially reusable structure. Learning can ask which parts remain informative, where the reasoning breaks, and how a successful continuation differs.

The policy transition addresses a second challenge: supervision should improve the model’s own competence rather than create permanent dependence on privileged context. Studying both stages helps distinguish gains from access to an expert attempt and gains that persist in the model’s independent reasoning.
